q: Explain dram-shop liability and how you would structure a beverage programme around it.
accept: liability for serving a visibly intoxicated guest managed by certification refusal protocols and insurance
dram shop laws make the licence holder liable so train staff document refusals and insure
civil liability for over service handled through training documented incidents and liquor liability cover
ans: Dram-shop statutes make the licensee civilly liable for harm a guest causes third parties after being served while visibly intoxicated, or after being served a minor. Most states have some version, whether by statute or through common-law negligence; a handful — Nevada is the standard example — provide essentially no such cause of action. Social-host provisions can extend exposure to private events and off-site catering. Structurally: certify every server, bartender and manager under the recognised programme, whether TIPS, ServSafe Alcohol, California's RBS or Texas's TABC; write and rehearse a refusal-of-service protocol so that refusal is a house decision carried out by a manager rather than a server's personal confrontation; set a written ID standard; keep an incident log with times, names and signatures; control the pour through measured service and stated tasting-menu pour sizes so a pairing is not an open bar; arrange transport and food; and carry liquor-liability insurance, which most carriers discount for certified staff. Then police the culture, because a room where refusing a guest costs a server their table is a room where nobody refuses.
exp: This is the question where a sommelier's answer must sound like a manager's. The examiner is testing two things: that you know the liability attaches to the licence holder rather than to the individual server, and that documentation is the defence.

q: Write a corkage policy for a fine-dining room and defend it economically.
accept: set a fee that covers lost margin limit bottles bar duplicates waive one per bottle bought and check state law
charge a fee limit the bottles waive corkage with a list purchase
corkage prices the service limit bottles waive on purchase and confirm legality
~covers the contribution margin lost
~covers the lost contribution margin
~fee that covers the lost margin
~the fee the limits and the exceptions
ans: State the fee, the limits and the exceptions. Set a fee that at least covers the contribution margin lost on a mid-list bottle — in practice, near the price of an entry bottle on your own list. Limit it to one or two bottles per table, require that the wine not already appear on the list, restrict formats and vintages to what the room can properly serve, and waive one corkage for every bottle purchased from the list. Reserve the right to decline during peak service and on holidays, and publish the policy so nobody negotiates at the table. Economically, corkage looks like forfeited margin but is not: the table bringing a bottle is usually a collector who then orders from the list, occupies a seat that would generate the same food spend regardless, and consumes exactly the same stemware, polishing, decanting and floor labour — so the fee prices the service, not the wine. The waiver clause converts the policy from a toll into an upsell. Check the law first: BYO is state-regulated, prohibited outright in some jurisdictions, and the licence generally governs whether outside alcohol may be consumed on the premises at all.
exp: The commonest error is treating corkage as a punishment for disloyalty. Priced to cover service and waived intelligently, it recruits precisely the guests who spend the most on wine across a year — and a hostile policy simply sends them to the restaurant next door.

q: An owner asks why you don't simply import your wines yourself. Give the real comparison.
accept: better margin and exclusivity set against licensing cash tied up freight risk and container minimums
direct import saves the wholesaler margin but adds permits minimums and cash exposure
margin and exclusivity versus compliance capital and logistics so run a hybrid
ans: Direct import buys two things: margin, because you pay FOB rather than a wholesaler's price, and exclusivity, because the label is yours alone and the story sells itself. Against that, count the costs honestly. You need a federal importer's basic permit and COLA label approvals, and in most states the wine must still move through a licensed wholesaler — three-tier does not dissolve because you paid the producer — so you either accept a middle-tier margin or acquire the permits and the compliance burden yourself. You buy at container scale, which may be a year's supply of a wine you cannot return; you pay months before the wine arrives, so working capital sits on the water; you carry currency exposure between order and settlement; you need reefer freight and you own the risk of a cooked container; you need insurance, bonded storage and someone to file entries. And there is no rep to call when a case arrives short. The honest answer is usually a hybrid: direct-import two or three high-volume, high-margin house pours where velocity and cash flow are predictable, and keep the distributor relationships for depth, allocations, and the ability to buy six bottles on a Tuesday.
exp: The comparison the examiner wants is capital and risk, not romance. Emphasise the three-tier point in particular: in most states a restaurant cannot take title directly from a foreign producer without a licensed wholesaler somewhere in the chain, and owners routinely assume otherwise.

q: Explain the Napa Valley Agricultural Preserve — what it did, when, and how it has been kept in place.
accept: 1968 zoning that protected farmland from development with minimum parcel sizes
the first us agricultural preserve in 1968 locked in by measure j and measure p
agricultural zoning from 1968 requiring a countywide vote to rezone
1968 ag preserve forty acre minimums with voter protection to 2058
ans: Adopted in 1968, it was the first agricultural preserve in the United States: the county zoned the valley floor for agriculture as its highest and best use, set minimum parcel sizes — now 40 acres on the floor and 160 in the hills — and effectively barred subdivision and residential or commercial sprawl on farmland. Zoning can normally be undone by a board of supervisors, so Napa locked it: Measure J in 1990 required a countywide popular vote to rezone agricultural land, and Measure P in 2008 extended that requirement to 2058. The result is that a valley within an hour's drive of San Francisco is still planted rather than paved, and that vineyard land is priced as an asset nobody can manufacture more of.
exp: Land-use law functioning as terroir policy. The counterfactual is the Santa Clara Valley, whose orchards and vineyards had no such protection and became Silicon Valley. This is also the honest half of the answer to 'why does Napa Cabernet cost what it does' — the constraint is legal as much as agricultural.
